48cb496e570795db: KUALA LUMPUR: The justification for introducing a new-generation MyKad, its security levels, and cooperation between Malaysia and Indonesia in tackling cross-border haze are among topics expected to take center stage during the Dewan Rakyat sitting today.

According to the Order Paper, during the question-and-answer session, Mohamad Shafizan Kepli (GPS-Batang Lupar) will ask the home minister to explain the extent to which enhanced security features, chip technology, and identity verification systems on the new MyKad can combat forgery, cloning, and the misuse of citizens' identities, while ensuring their personal data remains protected.

Datuk Iskandar Dzulkarnain Abdul Khalid (Kuala Kangsar) wants the Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability to explain the diplomatic actions and cooperation implemented by the Malaysian government with the Indonesian government to mitigate the risk of cross-border haze.

Also expected to draw attention is a question from Yeo Bee Yin (PH-Puchong) to the investment, trade and industry regarding the latest status minister of the initiative to produce 60,000 skilled workers in the semiconductor field under the National Semiconductor Strategy (NSS), including the number of individuals trained and the budget spent so far.

Datuk Mas Ermieyati Samsudin (Bersatu-Masjid Tanah) will ask the entrepreneur development and cooperatives minister to state the percentage of micro-entrepreneurs who received financing and assistance from the ministry's agencies from 2023 to 2026, those who successfully upgraded their business category to small or medium enterprises (SMEs), and the business failure rate after three years.

Additionally, Zahir Hassan (PH-Wangsa Maju) will pose a question to the transport minister regarding the full implementation schedule of the open payment system for all public transportation services in the Klang Valley.

Following the question-and-answer session, the sitting is scheduled to proceed with the tabling of the Registration of Criminals and Undesirable Persons (Amendment) Bill 2026 for its first reading by the home minister.

The sitting will then resume the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 at the policy stage following the tabling of 2027 Budget by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also the finance minister, on Oct 9.

Based on the calendar for the Third Meeting of the Fifth Session of the 15th Parliament, the policy-stage debate on 2027 Budget runs from Oct 12 to 22, prior to the winding-up sessions by relevant ministers for four days beginning Oct 26.
The Dewan Rakyat sitting will run for 37 days until Dec 8.
3e820c442764d9a1: TITUSVILLE/HOUSTON: Two top US Energy Department officials said on Tuesday they were working with refiners at home and abroad to boost fuel output as a diesel shortage has raised prices, driving dissatisfaction among voters with the White House ahead of the November midterm elections.

Diesel prices have jumped to record highs because of disruptions from the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries . Retail diesel prices averaged about US$6.32 a gallon on Tuesday, according to motorist group AAA.

The Trump administration has taken several steps to try to lower fuel prices that have surged since the start of the Iran war on Feb 28, including relaxing restrictions on Russian diesel exports, invoking the Defense Production Act to boost output and allowing commercial vehicles to run on red-dyed diesel normally limited to off-road equipment.

Diesel is critical to the global economy, powering much of the transport, agriculture and heavy industry that underpin global trade and economic activity. The high cost of fuel has soured voters on US President Donald Trump's stewardship of the economy, with 36 per cent approving of Trump on that issue, according to the most recent Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll.

"We are talking about reopening every refinery we can," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in Houston. "There are dialogues there, and that's a tough challenge. I'm not saying all these are going to happen."
DIFFICULT TO RAISE US OUTPUT
US refineries are running near full capacity, and with several facilities shutting in recent years, there is little leeway to quickly boost domestic output, analysts say.
Refinery expansions are capital intensive and take months, if not years, to complete depending on the complexity of the additions.
Wright said the US is also working with India to increase refining output there to bring products to global markets.

American Petroleum Institute chief executive officer Mike Sommers told Reuters on the sidelines of an energy forum in Titusville, Pennsylvania that US refiners are running at 95 per cent to 100 per cent of capacity. He said they are putting off planned maintenance because of high prices.

"The American refiners are doing everything they can," Sommers said. He said that using the Defense Production Act to restart idled plants, as the administration has floated, would require a lot of capital.
Last week, Vice President JD Vance said the administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings.
Trump signed legislation last year that included US$1 billion in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.
Wright said there was "more to do" on refining and the Defense Production Act but did not provide additional details.

Sommers singled out China's spare refining capacity, saying their government is currently barring diesel exports. Beijing "is really going to be the key if we're going to get long-term prices down," he said.

A spokesperson for theChinese embassy in Washington said the key to resolving the issue is to achieve a ceasefire in Iran. "China stands ready to maintain communication with all sides to jointly safeguard global energy security and keep industrial and supply chains stable," the spokesperson added.
PUSH FOR EUROPEAN DIESEL

Trump temporarily waived sanctions this month on Russian diesel in an attempt to lower prices. Russian diesel will likely move to New England, if it moves to the US at all, Wright said. Already, cargoes from Russia are returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions, with two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil in recent days, Reuters reported on Tuesday.
The Trump administration has also been pushing Europe to release more fuel to balance global markets.

"We are working with our friends ... to find new and innovative ways to get more throughput" through refineries, said Energy Department Under Secretary Kyle Haustveit at the Drake Forum in Titusville.

While the Trump administration has pushed Europe to release 50 million barrels of diesel, an agreement by industrialised nations fell short of that target. The Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) said last week it would speed the release of crude ​and oil product volumes pledged in March, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible.

Fatih Birol, chief of the IEA, which coordinates industrialised nations' releases ​of oil from emergency stocks, said on Tuesday the group ‌is ready to coordinate more oil releases by member countries if needed.

676c944a1cbf9f75: MUNICH: Bayern winger Serge Gnabry is not surprised former teammate Mikel Arteta became a successful coach, saying the Arsenal boss was always a leader in the dressing room.
Gnabry, who started his club career at Arsenal, will go up against Arteta's Gunners at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday in the Champions League.
"He was certainly a leader within our team back then. He was the captain during the season we played together," Gnabry told reporters on Tuesday.
"I remember him helping us out. He shared a lot of advice with us. He was always very approachable and open.
"That just goes to show what a kind person he is. He led the team to great success. It's not that we saw it coming, but he's clearly developed further and has done a fantastic job."
The 31-year-old Germany international admitted it was "strange" to face a team coached by a former teammate, but added: "It's a special match for me - playing against my former club.
"The club where I spent many years, I grew up there from the age of 16."
Already without the suspended Michael Olise and the injured Jamal Musiala, Bayern come into the match with doubts around coach Vincent Kompany, captain Manuel Neuer and midfielder Joshua Kimmich.

Kompany is suffering from a virus and may not be in the dugout, while Neuer is fighting to return from injury and Kimmich, who would captain the side in Neuer's absence, missed Tuesday's training due to personal reasons.
English assistant coach Aaron Danks took Tuesday's press conference and could step in for Kompany on Wednesday, but said there would be no extra personal motivation for the match.

"I think it's always Bayern Munich's victory. I know Vince would be really strong on this, it's never about anybody's individual achievements, it's always about the collective, about the group," he said.
"When you come to work with a club like Bayern Munich, you know it's much bigger than all of us."
Kompany was on the sidelines for Saturday's 6-1 win over RB Leipzig in the Bundesliga but had difficulty walking and did not take the post-match press conference.
"For me, not too much changes," Danks said.
"I plan the training sessions every day, and I take quite a lead on the grass. Obviously, when Vincent's not with us, we miss him, we miss having him around...
"You have to really get him to rest, but it's a challenge. You know him as a person, he's a real leader, he works hard, so it's important that he rests."
bd4e26d4259f677a: SEPANG: Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain arrived at the court complex to face two charges over an alleged assault involving two Special Branch policemen.
Security was tight at the court complex, with a heavy presence of police personnel and Rela members.
Only court staff and police personnel were allowed to park within the compound.
Shuhaily, dressed in a suit, appeared in high spirits as he walked into the canteen for breakfast, even inviting journalists and photographers to join him.
Also present in a show of solidarity was Port Klang MCBA commander Datuk Nik Ezanee Mohd Faisal.

Shuhaily, 54, is expected to face two charges of voluntarily causing hurt to Lance Corporals Mohammad Faiz Muhamad Saman, 40, and Muhammad Ekmal Sofwan Driman in connection with a Sept 28 incident at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 1.
The charges, under Section 323 of the Penal Code, carry a maximum jail term of one year, a fine of up to RM2,000, or both, upon conviction.
Shuhaily will be represented by lawyer Kitson Foong.

On Oct 17, Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) had requested further clarification and additional investigative work before deciding on the next course of action.
He said police had been directed to complete the investigation in accordance with the AGC's requirements.
The investigation papers were initially submitted to the AGC after police recorded statements from 25 witnesses.
Attorney-General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said he received the papers on Oct 6 before returning them to police on Oct 8.
On Oct 12, Faiz lodged a second police report alleging that his mobile phone had been seized while he was taking photographs of the incident.
His lawyers, Kamal Hisham Ja'afar and Muhammad Nor Tamrin, said the report contained new evidence.
The two policemen, who were serving as travel control officers at the airport, have denied allegations that they were acting as touts or involved in "counter setting".
The incident drew public attention after a video circulated online showing a man resembling Shuhaily berating two men at the airport. One of the men appeared to be grabbed forcefully by the ears.
On Oct 1, Shuhaily said he was prepared to accept whatever decision the government made over the incident and was ready to take responsibility for his actions.
be44f1f11cb5364a: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's defending men's team champions staged a remarkable fightback to keep their title defence alive as both national squads advanced to the knockout stage of the IBF World Cup in Munich on Tuesday.
The qualifying rounds, held over two days, saw both Malaysian teams finish strongly to secure their places in the last 16.

After winning just two of their opening six matches in Group D, the quartet of Rafiq Ismail, Timmy Tan, Tun Hakim Tun Hasnul Azam and Ahmad Muaz Fishol produced five consecutive victories to snatch the fourth and final qualifying spot on Tuesday.
The Malaysians defeated Kuwait, Guatemala, the Netherlands, Serbia and Cyprus, all by 2-0 margins, to finish with seven wins and four defeats for 21 points.
They ended level with Denmark and the Netherlands but prevailed in a roll-off to secure their place in the last 16.
Rafiq and Co won the tightly contested roll off 192 to Denmark's 182 and Netherlands 177.
Malaysian Tenpin Bowling Congress (MTBC) secretary-general Maradona Chok praised the quartet's determination after their difficult start.

"The boys showed tremendous character. They knew they were in a difficult position, but they never gave up. To win five matches in a row when it mattered most says a lot about their fighting spirit," said Maradona.
Their reward is a challenging encounter against Group A winners Qatar today, with a quarter-final berth at stake.

It was a timely return to form for the same quartet who made history by capturing Malaysia's maiden men's team gold at last year's World Cup in Hong Kong, where they defeated Puerto Rico 3-2 in the final.

The strong finish also provided a welcome boost after all four failed to reach the knockout stage of the singles competition, with Rafiq, last year's silver medallist, coming closest following a dramatic roll-off defeat.
"This is the same team that made history last year. They know what it takes to win at this level, and hopefully, they can carry this momentum into the knockout rounds," Maradona added.

Meanwhile, the national women's team were equally impressive, finishing third in Group B with 33 points after recording 11 wins and just two defeats across 13 rounds, including two automatic victories from byes.

Led by newly crowned singles silver medallist Natasha Roslan, the team comprising Sin Li Jane, Adelia Nur Irwan Syazalee and Nur Hazirah Ramli finished behind unbeaten Macao, China (39 points) and Sweden (33).
The Malaysians lost their opening match to Sweden and another to Macau, but otherwise enjoyed a productive qualifying campaign.
They closed with five straight 2-0 victories over Greece, the Netherlands, the Czech Republic, Poland and China to comfortably secure their place among the last 16.
The women will face Australia in today's knockout round as they seek to extend their impressive run and move a step closer to another World Cup medal.

"The girls have also done exceptionally well. Natasha's silver was a great start, and the team have shown they are hungry for more. Both teams are still in the fight, and that's exactly where we want to be," said Maradona.
Natasha narrowly missed out on defending her women's singles crown after losing 2-1 to France's Manon Clement in Sunday's final.
The Malaysian women also have unfinished business after finishing runners-up to the United States at last year's World Cup, losing a closely contested final 3-2.
With both national teams through, Malaysia remain in contention for a golden finish to their campaign, with the quarter-finals, semi-finals and finals scheduled for Wednesday.

a7818ca77c19cd51: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysians will benefit from wider access to affordable essentials, improved distribution in rural areas and stronger consumer protection under the 2027 Budget, as the government steps up efforts to address the rising cost of living.
The RM80 billion allocation for aid, subsidies and incentives aims to ease financial pressures on households while supporting businesses, rural entrepreneurs and the creative industry.

The measures, backed by additional funding for affordable sales programmes and enforcement, intends to make essential goods more accessible, improve market fairness and create new economic opportunities.
The allocation for the Program Jualan Rahmah Madani (PJRM) and Program Jualan Agro Madani will increase from RM630 million to RM750 million, supporting 35,000 sales events nationwide.
The fund will cover 30,000 Rahmah Sales programmes and 5,000 Agro Sales programmes.
The Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry will prioritise rural communities, low-cost housing areas and People's Housing Programme developments.
Greater participation by grocery shops and vending machine operators, alongside wholesale sales events, will make discounted goods more accessible.
For households, this means more opportunities to purchase necessities at lower prices.

Small traders are expected to benefit from the PJRM Borong, which aims to improve access to supplies and reduce inventory costs. Lower operating costs can help traders sustain their businesses and offer goods at more competitive prices.
BETTER ACCESS IN RURAL AREAS
An allocation of RM250 million to expand the distribution of essential goods to rural and remote areas will help address supply challenges faced by underserved communities.
The initiative will cover six new locations: Kampung Buayan, Kampung Terian, Kaiduan, Kundasang and Kampung Nibang in Sabah, as well as Kampung Dato Godam in Sarawak.
More reliable distribution networks can reduce the need for rural folk to travel long distances to obtain necessities, easing their transport costs and logistical burdens.
The initiative aims to narrow the gap between urban and remote communities in terms of access to essential goods.
NEW OPPORTUNITIES FOR BUSINESSES

Rural entrepreneurs stand to benefit from the RM10 million allocation for Jom Beli Produk Malaysia (Jom Malaysia), formerly known as Kempen Beli Barangan Malaysia, to encourage people to support Malaysian products.
The initiative will help businesses promote their products and high-value services through digital platforms and explore domestic and international markets.
For small businesses with limited market access, greater online exposure can help them reach more customers, increase sales and develop new revenue streams.
Consumers can contribute to the growth of local businesses by choosing Malaysian products, while entrepreneurs gain opportunities to expand their customer base.
STRONGER CONSUMER PROTECTION AND FAIRER MARKETS
The 2027 Budget provides RM1.1 billion to strengthen agencies' enforcement capabilities, including the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry and the Malaysia Competition Commission.
The allocation is intended to improve compliance with trade and competition laws, protect consumers and address offences within the jurisdictions of these authorities.
For consumers, more effective enforcement can help safeguard their interests and promote fairer market practices.
The government also plans to table an E-commerce Bill at the next Parliament sitting to strengthen oversight of online platforms and sellers, including foreign operators.

As online shopping becomes more common, the proposed legislation aims to improve accountability and consumer safety while helping micro, small and medium enterprises compete in a fairer digital marketplace.
FOOD DONATIONS AND WASTE REDUCTION

Tax deductions for food and equipment donations to the Ihsan Food Bank Initiative (i-FB), applicable from Jan 1, 2027 to Dec 31, 2030, are intended to encourage businesses to support food redistribution.
The initiative adopts a 3S approach - "Santuni Komuniti, Sayangi Alam, Selamatkan Makanan" (Care for Communities, Love the Environment, Save Food).
By encouraging businesses to donate usable food and equipment, the measure can help direct resources to communities in need while reducing food waste and promoting more responsible resource use.
SUPPORTING CREATIVE TALENT
The government aims to develop 20 new animation intellectual properties and commercialise Malaysian characters internationally.
The initiative can create opportunities for Malaysian creators and businesses to develop marketable content, secure licensing deals and reach audiences abroad.
Stronger intellectual property protection and registration will help creators safeguard their work and increase its commercial value, benefiting businesses in production and related services.
TURNING ALLOCATIONS INTO TANGIBLE BENEFITS
The 2027 Budget's measures cover several aspects of Malaysians' daily lives, from household spending and access to basic necessities to business opportunities and online consumer protection.
Households can benefit from more affordable goods, while rural communities stand to gain from improved distribution.
Small businesses and entrepreneurs can access new markets, while consumers can benefit from stronger enforcement and greater accountability in online transactions.
But the extent of these benefits will depend on effective implementation, with the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry playing a key role in ensuring initiatives reach intended recipients.

Through its efforts to improve access to affordable essentials, strengthen consumer protection, enforce trade regulations and support businesses, the ministry will be instrumental in translating 2027 Budget allocations into tangible benefits for households and businesses.

Ultimately, the success of these measures will depend on how effectively the ministry and other agencies implement initiatives to ease the cost of living, promote fairer market practices and strengthen the competitiveness of the domestic economy.

e7851033e13b011a: PETALING JAYA: Any national database on femicide must track previous reports of domestic abuse, stalking and missed opportunities for intervention to help authorities identify patterns of escalating violence before they turn fatal, says a lawyer group.

Association of Women Lawyers (AWL) vice-president Denise Lim told FMT this could help authorities identify recurring themes and protection failures instead of treating each killing as an isolated incident.
She said treating gender-related killings as ordinary homicides risked overlooking warning signs, particularly when a woman sought to leave an abusive relationship.

The Women’s Aid Organisation (WAO) recently renewed its push for Malaysia to legally recognise femicide — defined as the intentional, gender-motivated killings of women and girls — following a series of such cases nationwide over the past year.

WAO called for systematic tracking of femicide, warning that cases risked being treated as isolated homicides rather than patterns rooted in misogyny, possessiveness and coercive control without a specific legal or statistical category for such killings.

Lim said a systematic record of repeated complaints, and a perpetrator’s history of escalating behaviour — such as intimidation, stalking and threats — could help authorities identify cases requiring urgent intervention.

She also called for police to be trained to recognise non-physical forms of abuse, such as psychological and emotional abuse, financial control and coercive behaviour, as well as intimidation tactics such as harming a victim’s pets.
Lim said domestic violence was often dismissed as a private family matter, discouraging victims from seeking help.
“Domestic violence must not be dismissed as merely ‘perkara rumah tangga’. This trivialises abuse and discourages victims from seeking help,” she said.
Several countries have established femicide observatories or similar mechanisms to analyse gender-based killings and identify gaps in protection.

They include South Africa’s Femicide Watch, Argentina’s National Femicide Registry and Spain’s Observatory on Violence against Women, as well as mechanisms in Georgia, Slovakia, Palestine, Ecuador and Morocco.

Parent Action Group for Education (PAGE) chairman Noor Azimah Abdul Rahim called for practical workshops and resources to help parents teach children about personal boundaries, rather than relying on annual awareness campaigns.
She said schools and parents needed a shared understanding of unacceptable behaviour and how to respond when it occurred.

Azimah also called for clearer referral procedures involving the education ministry, police, social welfare department and health authorities so families knew which agencies were responsible for handling reports of harassment, stalking and threats.
She said parents would regain trust in schools only when complaints led to meaningful action rather than administrative delays.
“Schools should not wait for a situation to become a tragedy before recognising that the warning signs mattered,” she added.
48e2dda8d329f466: PETALING JAYA: More Malaysians are formalising what should happen to their money and assets after they are gone, but that has not necessarily made them feel more secure about the future.

A recent survey found that 37% of Malaysian respondents fully documented and communicated their legacy plans in 2026, up sharply from 15% last year. This marked the highest proportion among the six Asian markets surveyed, while the share of Malaysians with no legacy plan at all fell from 23% to 10%.

The research, conducted in August, surveyed 3,073 people across Hong Kong, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam. The Malaysian sample comprised 506 respondents across different generations and wealth levels.

Yet greater organisation has not erased one big concern: whether the wealth being passed on will actually endure. Among Malaysians intending to leave financial assets or wealth, 80% worried that it might not survive beyond the next generation, compared with 70% across the region.

Market volatility topped the list of Malaysian concerns at 54%, followed by whether beneficiaries were ready to manage inherited wealth at 49%. Family conflict came next at 47%, while 37% cited possible legal, regulatory or tax changes.

Those findings suggest that legacy planning is about more than deciding who gets what. Documentation is only one part of preparedness: families also need to consider whether their intentions are understood and whether future beneficiaries are ready for what they may inherit.

Millennials were especially conflicted. Among those planning to leave financial assets or wealth, 90% worried it might not last beyond the next generation, compared with 82% of Gen Z respondents and 71% of both Gen X and baby boomers.

At the same time, millennials were the most optimistic about the long-term impact of what they leave behind: 69% believed their legacy would have a positive effect for generations to come, compared with 47% of Gen Z, 53% of Gen X and 48% of baby boomers.

What Malaysians hope to leave behind is also revealing. Education was the most commonly selected legacy priority, with 51% placing it among their top three, ahead of wealth at 49% and family traditions at 44%.

Among those intending to leave financial assets or wealth, 53% wanted the money invested for long-term growth, 52% wanted it used to support family members during their lifetime, and 50% hoped it would fund education. This suggests inheritance is often being thought of less as a lump sum and more as something intended to keep working for the family.

Communication, however, still appears incomplete. While 66% said older generations in their families had communicated at least some aspects of their plans, only 32% said those plans had been explained fully.

Formal family meetings were the most common setting for these conversations, at 51%, while 40% said discussions were more informal. The share communicating through financial advisers also rose from 16% in 2025 to 31% this year.

A will remains one of the basic tools for distributing assets - it allows a person to set out how assets such as property, vehicles, shares and investments should be distributed, while also appointing an executor to carry out those wishes.

But the new survey suggests that written instructions alone do not answer every question. Families may still need to consider whether beneficiaries understand the plan, whether they are prepared to manage what they receive, and what the money is ultimately meant to achieve.

That may explain why Malaysians can be both more organised and more anxious at the same time. Putting a legacy plan on paper is a significant first step, but keeping that legacy intact may depend just as much on what happens after the documents are signed.
f7d3031ea5d67157: Saya kira Perikatan Nasional hanya boleh menyalahkan diri sendiri apabila pendaftarannya dibatalkan oleh Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia (JPPM atau RoS). Saya yakin JPPM punya alasan kukuh berdasarkan undang-undang untuk lakukan apa yang ia lakukan.

Bagi Setiausaha Agung Bersatu Azmin Ali, pembatalan pendaftaran PN membuktikan aduan partinya kepada JPPM terhadap pimpinan PN memang berasas. Bersatu mengadu kepimpinan PN yang dipengerusikan PAS telah menafikan hak Bersatu untuk menghadiri, memberi pendapat dan mengundi dalam mesyuarat majlis tertinggi PN pada 16 Julai lalu. Ini menurut Azmin ialah pelanggaran fasal 7.1 perlembagaan PN.

Kata penganalisis politik Sivamurugan Pandian, the RoS decision is not merely an administrative issue tetapi membawa implikasi significant ke atas kestabilan politik gabungan itu dan juga persediaannya menghadapi pilihan raya.
"Politically it may weaken public confidence and intensify tensions among component parties particularly over leadership and the coalition's future direction," kata Siva.

Kata beliau, the real impact bergantung pada apa yang berlaku on the ground, keputusan berhubung apa-apa rayuan yang dibuat (PN diberitakan akan mencabar tindakan JPPM) serta kemampuan kepimpinannya mengekalkan perpaduan.

"Ultimately this is a test of PN's political resilience. How quickly and collectively its leaders respond will determine whether the crisis weakens the coalition or becomes an opportunity for internal restructuring," Begitu pandangan Siva dan memang ada benarnya.

Yang pasti PN khususnya PAS akan play victim. Seperti ketika JPPM menggantung semua aktivitinya pada Sept lalu dan memberinya kesempatan untuk menjawab surat tunjuk sebab mengapa ia tidak perlu dibatalkan. Obviously, RoS is not satisfied with PN's sebab-sebab. Ketika itu PN beri gambaran ia dijadikan mangsa permainan politik kerajaan. Sekarang taktik itu diperhebatkan. Tidak perlu saya ulangi apa yang sedang diperkatakan oleh kepimpinannya (baca: PAS).

Bagi penyokong PN, yang mesti dipersalahkan ialah Pakatan Harapan, apatah lagi tindakan JPPM muncul menjelang PRN Melaka. Kesalahan PN sendiri yang membawa kepada tindakan RoS is conveniently forgotten. Ringkasnya PN dibatalkan, ramai belasah PH. Jika PN rugi, dan begitu juga PH, maka siapa yang dapat untung?
"Sebenarnya yang paling untung daripada pembatalan PN ialah BN," kata Yusri Ibrahim, ketua penyelidik Ilham Centre.
Kata beliau, yang bunuh BN pada PRU dan beberapa PRN lalu ialah PN. "Mereka bertembung di segmen yang sama iaitu segmen Melayu. Tetapi Umno boleh berdepan PAS kecuali di Kelantan dan Terengganu."
Di dua negeri Pantai Timur itu, PAS reign supreme. Logo PAS digunakan untuk dapatkan undi dengan jaya. Semua orang kenal dan terima bulan. But not outside Kelantan and Terengganu.

Maka jenama PN digunakan. "Bila ada jenama PN di luar Terengganu dan Kelantan bercampur dengan confidence level Muhyiddin Yassin dan partinya Bersatu untuk segmen Melayu, undi Melayu BN pergi ke PN," kata Yusri.

Ertinya logo bulan PAS sukar 'dijual' di kawasan Melayu di luar Kelantan dan Terengganu tetapi logo PN diterima. Melayu yang undi BN boleh dibaca sebagai mereka tidak mahu PAS tetapi boleh undi PN walaupun PAS ada di dalamnya -- pelik tapi benar gamaknya.

Singkatnya logo PN ada nilai di luar Kelantan, Terengganu dan mungkin juga Kedah. Sekarang logo PN tidak akan ada dalam kertas undi. Logo BN ada. Berdasarkan apa yang dikata Yusri, di situlah undi mereka akan hinggap.

PAS terpaksa guna logo sendiri di luar kubu kuat mereka. Komponen PN lain pun kena guna logo masing-masing. Logo PAS ramai juga orang kenal. Logo Gerakan ada juga yang tahu tetapi tidak boleh jana undi. Wawasan dan MIPP? Mungkin mereka terpaksa guna logo PAS.
Patutlah Yusri kata BN sedang ketawa dalam senyap.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
7d394798bc1370bb: WASHINGTON: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the United States hailed "very productive" talks in Oslo on Tuesday amid efforts to draw a line under a bitter feud between Kyiv's leader and US President Donald Trump over the war with Russia.
After talks with Trump's envoys in the Norwegian capital, Zelensky thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence of looming Russian strikes on civilian targets and energy plants.
Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff is now due to head from Oslo to Russia for talks with President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday in a bid to end Russia's four-year-old war on Ukraine.

The positive tone followed days of tensions between Kyiv and Washington since Trump struck a diesel-supply deal with Putin, and furiously called for Zelensky to be replaced after Ukraine refused to stop hitting Russian oil refineries.

"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelensky told reporters in Oslo. "I'm speaking about early warning, what is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming."
Flanked by Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb -- a golfing buddy of Trump -- Zelensky said it was "important that we keep the conversation going."

A US official told AFP after the talks that Zelensky held "very productive and constructive discussions" with businessman Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who took part remotely due to the flu.
"Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals," the official said.
'Make a deal'
But Trump kept up the pressure, saying at the White House that he wanted Zelensky to "make a deal" with Russia, which is escalating strikes on Ukraine as a bitter winter looms.
Trump, who last week called on Zelensky to resign, also criticised Zelensky for not accepting the terms he said he had offered during their infamous televised row in the Oval Office in February 2025.
Relations plunged back into a deep freeze earlier this month after Trump suddenly announced his deal with Russia for diesel, as part of his efforts to lower oil prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Ukraine reacted with dismay after Trump also waived sanctions against Russia's war machine and appeared to once again pivot to Putin.

The feud spiraled as Zelensky accused Trump of weakness, and then alleged that the United States was deliberately withholding vital intelligence and delaying the delivery of vital interceptor missiles.
Ukraine has also reported a reduction in speeds on Starshield, the US military satellite system which it uses for battlefield communications and strikes on Russian-occupied territory.
Trump has denied ordering a reduction in speeds on Starshield after Musk -- whose company SpaceX developed it -- said the order could only have come from the White House.
But the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that it was indeed Musk who ordered the slowdown in the military-grade version of Starlink.
'Our future'
The Oslo meeting followed furious diplomatic efforts in Washington, Kyiv and Western capitals to calm the situation.
Zelensky said earlier Tuesday he had held "substantive" talks with US secretary of state Marco Rubio.

Zelensky separately told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries, and that the shipment was waiting for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth's signature.
Several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval, he said.
Trump -- whose Republican party faces tough midterm elections amid dismal polling and high fuel prices -- has accused Zelensky of not trying to resolve the conflict with Russia.

Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war -- fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined.
Zelensky insisted Tuesday that Kyiv needed to be represented at any meeting regarding Ukraine's future.
"If there are issues about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It's absolutely clear," he said.
8edfafaf7e540a4c: PETALING JAYA: Bekas Menteri Perdagangan Indonesia, Muhammad Lutfi, membidas kenyataan Ahli Parlimen Muar Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman supaya Indonesia dilayan sebagai negara 'tersisih' dalam Asean susulan jerebu rentas sempadan yang berulang.
Lutfi berkata jerebu bukanlah peluang untuk mencari publisiti untuk meraih perhatian, ketika ribuan rakyat Indonesia juga terjejas dan ada anggota bomba terkorban ketika memadamkan kebakaran.

Katanya, syarikat Malaysia yang mengendalikan ladang di Indonesia juga perlu dipertanggungjawabkan terhadap krisis itu, dengan mendakwa kumpulan perladangan Malaysia menguasai sehingga 3.4 juta hektar tanah di negara itu dan sesetengahnya membiayai operasi mereka melalui bank Malaysia.

“Pastikan setiap syarikat yang melanggar peraturan dipertanggungjawabkan, sama ada syarikat Indonesia atau Malaysia. Namun, jangan sesekali menghina seluruh negara yang memberikan tanah dan lesen kepada industri anda untuk berkembang maju,” katanya di Instagram.

Lutfi berkata Amerika Syarikat sebelum ini pernah mengenakan sekatan import kepada pengeluar minyak sawit Malaysia seperti FGV Holdings dan Sime Darby Plantation, susulan dakwaan buruh paksa, namun Indonesia tidak pernah mengkritik Malaysia sebagai sebuah negara.
“Adakah Indonesia menganggap seluruh negara Malaysia sebagai negara tersisih kerana perkara itu? Tidak pernah,” katanya.
Beliau turut berkata laporan Greenpeace yang dirujuk oleh Syed Saddiq mengenai 19 titik panas kebakaran adalah di kawasan konsesi Indonesia yang dikaitkan dengan kumpulan Malaysia.
“Jika anda mahukan akauntabiliti, siasat syarikat-syarikat itu dan rantaian bekalan mereka.
“Jika anda tidak memahami cara perniagaan ini beroperasi, jangan jadikan seluruh negara saya sebagai sasaran,” katanya.

Lutfi berkhidmat sebagai menteri perdagangan Indonesia dari 14 Feb hingga 20 Okt 2014 di bawah Presiden Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, dan sekali lagi dari 23 Dis 2020 hingga 15 Jun 2022 di bawah Presiden Joko Widodo.

Syed Saddiq dalam perbahasan di Dewan Rakyat minggu lalu menggesa supaya Malaysia menggerakkan negara Asean untuk mengenakan tekanan diplomatik dan kewangan terhadap Indonesia berhubung masalah jerebu yang berulang.

Beliau juga menggesa supaya menghentikan pembiayaan kepada syarikat yang dikaitkan dengan pembakaran hutan dan menggerakkan pengguna untuk memberi tekanan kepada perniagaan yang terlibat dalam kebakaran itu.
“Anda perlu layan mereka sebagai negara tersisih di rantau ini,” kata Syed Saddiq.

Dalam hantaran Instagram berasingan, Lutfi turut menggesa Singapura meneliti penglibatan eksekutif dan kumpulan korporat yang berpangkalan di negara itu dalam syarikat Indonesia yang dikaitkan dengan kebakaran yang menyumbang kepada jerebu.

Pada Isnin, Agensi Alam Sekitar Kebangsaan Singapura (NEA) berkata pihaknya akan mengeluarkan notis kepada tiga lagi syarikat Indonesia berhubung kebakaran di Kalimantan, menjadikan jumlah keseluruhan syarikat yang disasarkan di bawah Akta Pencemaran Jerebu Rentas Sempadan (THPA) Singapura sebanyak 10.

Jerebu yang berpunca daripada asap kebakaran hutan di Indonesia menyelubungi beberapa kawasan di Malaysia dan Singapura sejak beberapa minggu ini, dengan cuaca kering berkaitan El Niño memburukkan lagi kebakaran tersebut.

Minggu lalu, jurucakap kerajaan Fahmi Fadzil berkata, berdasarkan semakan dengan syarikat-syarikat berkenaan, kebanyakan kebakaran yang dikesan di Indonesia berlaku di luar kawasan konsesi kelapa sawit milik syarikat Malaysia.
27ac844a50a77a64: LONDON: Former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag has accused Cristiano Ronaldo of letting the team down during his time in charge.
Portugal star Ronaldo was in his second spell at United when Ten Hag was hired in 2022.
Ten Hag's relationship with Ronaldo quickly became tense and the striker refused to come on as a substitute in a win over Tottenham in the October 2022.
Ronaldo was dropped for a subsequent match against Chelsea, prompting him to give an explosive television interview in which he said he felt betrayed by United and did not respect Ten Hag.
The former Real Madrid forward's contract at United was mutually terminated the following month.
"He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him," Ten Hag said in an interview with The Athletic.
"Obviously, he's one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in."
Ten Hag said Ronaldo pulled out of training sessions and did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign.

"I confronted him with this. Many times I say, 'Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can't bring yourself in the box, you can't score'. He was not capable to do this," Ten Hag said.
"It's the wrong idea to put this to me that I expected him to do the pressing, that he's exhausted. But he couldn't.
"He ran neither in possession nor out of possession. The reason was because he didn't prepare himself."
Ten Hag also claimed promises made by United's owners went unfulfilled before he was sacked in 2024, shortly after signing a new contract.
Although United won the FA Cup just months earlier with a surprise final victory against Manchester City, Ten Hag was axed with the team languishing in 14th place in the Premier League.
The Dutchman blamed the United hierarchy of some of his problems, saying he was left humiliated when Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent.
Ten Hag also said he wanted to sign Harry Kane, Declan Rice and Frenkie de Jong during his spell at United.
"They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn't keep," he said.
"I said, 'No selling Scott McTominay'. And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed."
193323d58acf1e1a: BRASILIA: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Tuesday pledged to disclose his bank, tax and telephone records as long as his right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro did the same, seeking to gain the upper hand as both grapple with graft allegations.

In a document submitted to Brazil's electoral court, Lula said he would authorise the release of his own bank, tax and telephone records, as well as those of his family members, if Flavio followed suit. The challenge extends to legal entities in which the two candidates are partners or directors, as well as entities whose bank accounts they are authorised to manage.

"The public disclosure of the banking, tax and telephone records of both candidates before next Wednesday is essential to ensure that the Brazilian people are properly informed and able to decide freely whom they will vote for," the document said.

Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the country's biggest-ever banking fraud with the now-defunct lender Banco Master. The probe focuses on an investment he allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the bank's owner, to help finance a film about his father.
The senator has acknowledged seeking funding but denies any wrongdoing. He is also under investigation in a separate probe over alleged money laundering.

Brazil's Supreme Court has authorised an investigation into Fabio Luis Lula da Silva, one of Lula's sons, over alleged influence peddling and corruption tied to health ministry dealings, as well as a separate pension-fraud probe. Lula's son denies the allegations and the president has said his son would be treated like any other citizen.

"I'm willing to let Brazilians see who the thieves and corrupt people in this country really are. I want to see whether he (Bolsonaro) has the courage to disclose his bank and phone records," Lula said during a campaign event in Maranhao state.

The move was not intended to prove the president's innocence but to demonstrate that "those with nothing to hide have nothing to fear," according to Lula's Workers' Party communications secretary Eden Valadares.
Flavio Bolsonaro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
77027e9d69bd9918: PETALING JAYA: An independent scholar and a former deputy minister have attributed the rise in religious intolerance among schoolchildren to the growing trend of communal politics.
Scholar Sharifah Munirah Alatas and former deputy unity minister Ti Lian Ker agreed that it was “hardly surprising” that MPs were now raising concerns about the trend.
Munirah said the reluctance of Muslim students to sit next to their non-Muslim classmates might appear to reflect a new level of intolerance in society, but past trends suggested otherwise.
Ethnocentrism, nativism, traditionalism and culturalism had been developing within the country’s Malay-Muslim political leadership for more than 50 years, she said.
Munirah lamented that ethnocentrism, nativism and traditionalism were now permeating society.

“When an MP points out the growing problem of religious and ethnic intolerance and polarisation in the classroom, I blame the ethnic and religiously charged political discourse that we have been seeing every day for decades,” she told FMT.
Munirah said such intolerance could be eradicated immediately and effectively if there was political will.
“But we all know that it is politically expedient to keep the siege mentality alive in society. It guarantees political ‘staying power’.”
Last Thursday, Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin raised concerns about intolerance among children, citing cases of primary school pupils refusing to sit with classmates who did not share their faith.
Some children, he told the Dewan Rakyat, did not want to sit next to others because they wore crosses or ate pork.
Ti, who served as deputy unity minister from 2020 to 2021, said he was not surprised by Willie’s remarks.

He said “something must have gone very wrong” if children insisted on sitting apart from classmates of different faiths. He added that, in the 1970s, children were allotted seats but there was no issue who ended up sitting with you.
Like Munirah, Ti also blamed communal politics for the division.

“Identity politics, as well as indoctrination and radicalisation by cybertroopers hired by political parties, has played a role in fostering intolerance among the people, who would then pass on such lessons to their children.”
To compound matters, these irresponsible cybertroopers, who push incendiary narratives, seemed to be immune to the law, Ti said.
“This group of people would view every incident through a racial lens and pit two races against each other,” he added.
34873e858f68950f: PETALING JAYA: Seorang cendekiawan bebas dan bekas timbalan menteri mengaitkan peningkatan sikap tidak toleran terhadap agama dalam kalangan murid sekolah dengan trend politik kemasyarakatan berlaku kini.
Cendekiawan Sharifah Munirah Alatas dan bekas timbalan menteri perpaduan, Ti Lian Ker, bersetuju 'tidak mengejutkan' apabila Ahli Parlimen mula membangkitkan kebimbangan mengenai trend berkenaan.
Munirah berkata, keengganan murid Islam duduk di sebelah rakan sekelas bukan Islam, mungkin terlihat tahap baru toleransi rendah dalam masyarakat.
Katanya, etnosentrisme, nativisme, tradisionalisme, dan kulturalisme telah berkembang dalam kalangan kepimpinan politik Melayu-Islam negara ini lebih 50 tahun.
Munirah kecewa kerana etnosentrisme, nativisme, dan tradisionalisme mula meresap dalam masyarakat.

“Apabila seorang Ahli Parlimen membangkitkan masalah tiada toleransi dan polarisasi agama serta etnik yang semakin meningkat dalam bilik darjah, saya menyalahkan wacana politik berbaur etnik dan agama yang kita saksikan saban hari sejak puluhan tahun,” katanya kepada FMT.
Munirah berkata, sikap sedemikian boleh dibasmi secara berkesan sekiranya ada iltizam politik.
“Tetapi, kita semua tahu bahawa segi politik (parti politik) mahu mengekalkan 'mentaliti terkepung' dalam masyarakat. Ia menjamin 'daya tahan politik'.”

Khamis lalu, Ahli Parlimen Puncak Borneo Willie Mongin membangkitkan kebimbangan sikap tidak toleran dalam kalangan kanak-kanak, sambil memetik kes murid sekolah rendah enggan duduk bersama rakan sekelas tidak seagama.
Katanya di Dewan Rakyat, ada kanak-kanak tidak mahu duduk bersebelahan rakan lain kerana rakan memakai salib atau makan babi.
Ti, yang pernah berkhidmat sebagai timbalan menteri perpaduan dari 2020 hingga 2021, berkata beliau tidak terkejut apa disebut Willie.

Beliau berkata 'pasti ada sesuatu sangat tidak kena' sekiranya kanak-kanak berkeras mahu duduk berasingan daripada rakan sekelas berlainan agama. Beliau berkata, pada 1970-an, tempat duduk murid telah ditetapkan dan tidak pernah timbul isu siapa duduk di sebelah.

7da8ef388262f2ef: PETALING JAYA: The idea of establishing food banks for elephants might initially sound rather unconventional, but it could offer a practical response to one of Malaysia's increasingly complex wildlife conservation challenges.

As expanding agricultural activities and fragmented forest habitats bring elephants into closer contact with human settlements, authorities are exploring ways to reduce these encounters without compromising the animals' welfare.

On Oct 17, the Perak government announced that it was studying a proposal to establish dedicated elephant feeding areas and buffer zones near natural habitats, following a series of incursions into agricultural land.

State science, environment and green technology committee chairman Teh Kok Lim said the initiative would involve the state forestry department, as well as the department of wildlife and national parks.

By providing alternative food sources in strategically selected locations, authorities hope to discourage elephants from entering farms and residential areas, where their presence can result in extensive property damage and pose risks to both people and wildlife.
The proposal follows several incidents in Bukit Bangkong, Chemor, where elephants have repeatedly entered agricultural land in search of food.

According to Perhilitan, a group believed to comprise two or three elephants had been entering farms since Sept 27, prompting monitoring operations, overnight patrols and safety advisories for farm operators.
Twelve farmers subsequently sought assistance after approximately 9.7ha of agricultural land were damaged, illustrating the economic consequences of human-elephant conflict for rural communities.

Such incidents reflect a wider conservation dilemma. As forests become increasingly fragmented, elephants may find their traditional feeding grounds and movement corridors overlapping with plantations and settlements, bringing them into contact with communities that depend on the same land for their livelihoods.
Agricultural crops can also provide an accessible source of food for animals that spend much of their day foraging, making encounters difficult to prevent through conventional deterrents alone.
An alternative approach
While Perak's proposal remains under consideration, Johor has already implemented a programme establishing food banks along elephant movement corridors.

Rather than functioning as conventional food-distribution centres, these areas are planted with vegetation that elephants naturally consume, creating supplementary feeding grounds within designated habitats.
Banana plants and Napier grass have been cultivated at selected sites to encourage elephants to remain away from oil palm plantations and other agricultural areas.

The initiative began with three locations, each exceeding 1ha, including sites in Kluang. In July, the federal government announced plans to establish another 21 food banks in the state, extending the programme's potential reach.

The underlying principle is to reduce the incentive for elephants to enter cultivated land by ensuring suitable food sources remain available within safer areas. The approach could also complement conventional wildlife management measures, potentially reducing reliance on repeated capture and relocation when elephants stray into populated areas.

Nevertheless, the effectiveness of dedicated feeding areas will depend on careful planning and long-term monitoring, particularly given the extensive distances elephants can cover while searching for food.

Poorly positioned feeding sites could inadvertently concentrate animals near agricultural boundaries or alter their natural movement patterns, creating further complications rather than resolving existing ones.

Conservation strategies must, therefore, consider the relationship between food availability, habitat connectivity and elephant behaviour alongside practical measures such as barriers and protected movement corridors.

Equally important is recognising the competing interests involved: farmers need effective protection against crop damage and financial losses, while conservation authorities must safeguard a species whose survival depends on access to sufficiently large, connected habitats.

Ultimately, elephant food banks cannot substitute for broader habitat protection, but they may provide a useful supplementary measure within a more comprehensive approach to managing human-wildlife conflict.

For Perak, the challenge will be determining whether a model already being explored in Johor can be adapted to local conditions, helping rural communities and wild elephants coexist with fewer potentially dangerous encounters.
0349db5a536f2b84: PETALING JAYA: Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi has hit back at Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman over the Muar MP’s call to treat Indonesia as an "outcast" in Asean over the recurring transboundary haze.

Lutfi said the haze was not an opportunity for political grandstanding, and that Indonesian firefighters had died battling the blazes while hundreds of thousands of Indonesians were breathing in the smoke.

He argued that Malaysian companies operating plantations in Indonesia must also be held responsible for the crisis, claiming Malaysian plantation groups controlled up to 3.4 million hectares of land in the country while some financed their operations through Malaysian banks.
"Hold every rogue corporation accountable, whether Indonesian or Malaysian. But never insult an entire nation that gave your industries the land and licences to thrive," he said on Instagram.

Lutfi said while the US previously banned imports from Malaysian palm oil producers FGV Holdings and Sime Darby Plantation over allegedly forced labour, Indonesia had refrained from condemning Malaysia as a nation.
"Did Indonesia call the entire nation of Malaysia an outcast because of that? Never."
He also said the Greenpeace report Syed Saddiq cited during his debate identified 19 fire hotspots in Indonesian concessions linked to Malaysian groups.
"If you want accountability, investigate the companies and their supply chains," he said.
"If you don’t understand how this business works, don’t make my whole country a target."
Lutfi served as Indonesia’s trade minister from Feb 14 to Oct 20, 2014 under president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, and again from Dec 23, 2020 to June 15, 2022, under president Joko Widodo.
His remarks followed Syed Saddiq’s call in the Dewan Rakyat last week for Malaysia to rally Asean countries to exert diplomatic and financial pressure on Indonesia over the recurring haze.

Speaking during the 2027 budget debate, Syed Saddiq urged Malaysia to rally Asean against the haze, cut off financing to companies linked to open burning and mobilise consumers to pressure businesses implicated in the fires.
"You need to treat them as an outcast in the region," said Syed Saddiq.

In a separate Instagram post, Lutfi also called for Singapore to scrutinise the involvement of locally based executives and corporate groups in Indonesian companies linked to land fires that contribute to the haze.

On Monday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said it would issue notices to three additional Indonesian companies over fires in Kalimantan suspected of contributing to the haze in Singapore, bringing the total number of firms targeted under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act to 10.
Smoke from wildfires in Indonesia has blanketed parts of Malaysia and Singapore in recent weeks, with El Nino-related dry weather worsening the blazes.
Last week, government spokesman Fahmi Fadzil said most of the fires observed in Indonesia occurred outside oil palm concessions owned by Malaysian companies, according to checks with the firms.

7eac5dc4d24bb6eb: Malaysia's automotive industry has become an interesting battleground between Japan and China, two of the world's great carmaking powers. And the contest is being played out through our national carmakers, Proton and Perodua.
Proton has the backing of Zhejiang Geely, one of China's most technologically advanced automotive groups while Perodua has the support of Daihatsu and, behind it, the industrial might of Toyota.
Both partnerships have been successful, but the arrival of electric vehicles (EV) has changed the rules of the game.

China has taken a commanding lead in EV technology, battery production and manufacturing costs. Japan, despite its dominance of the global automotive industry for decades, has been more cautious about committing itself to battery electric vehicles beyond hybrids.
That puts Perodua in a particularly interesting position.

An important insight into Japan's intentions came in May when its ambassador to Malaysia, Noriyuki Shikata, described Perodua as one of the best examples of a successful Japanese-Malaysian joint venture. More significantly, he disclosed that Japan's economy, trade and industry ministry had decided to extend financial support for a new Perodua-led project.
Shikata also observed that Perodua was entering a new stage of innovation, developing solutions in Malaysia that Japan itself was interested in learning about.

Now, that is an interesting statement coming from the representative of one of the world's most sophisticated automotive nations. For more than three decades in the auto industry, we have regarded the Japanese as the teachers and Malaysians as the students.
Could the relationship now be evolving into something more equal?
From petrol to electric
Consider what Perodua has achieved.

Starting with the modest Kancil in 1994, it has grown into Malaysia's largest carmaker, commanding roughly 40% of our domestic market. Its success was built on affordable, reliable petrol-engine cars, efficient manufacturing and a formidable local supplier network.
The question is whether Perodua can translate these strengths into the electric age.

Its first home-grown EV, the QV-E, represents a bold but expensive undertaking. Unlike Proton, which can draw upon Geely's existing EV platforms and economies of scale, Perodua has invested heavily in developing its own product.
The difference is fundamental. Proton benefits from China's enormous EV ecosystem. Perodua is attempting to develop Malaysian engineering capabilities while building a new supply chain.
Market reception

The QV-E encountered a difficult market reception, with pricing and battery leasing arrangements initially raising questions among buyers. Subsequent price reductions have made it more competitive, but they also illustrate the formidable economics of EV manufacturing.
This is where government policy becomes important. Should Malaysia provide targeted financial assistance to Perodua to develop its EV capabilities?

I believe there is a strong case for doing so, provided the assistance is directed towards research, engineering, local components and technology development rather than simply subsidising car prices as China did for 5 years

There is an even stronger argument if Japan is prepared to participate. Toyota and Daihatsu possess enormous experience in manufacturing efficiency, quality control and supplier development. Combining these strengths with Perodua's local engineering ambitions could create something genuinely valuable.
It would also give Japan an opportunity to develop affordable EV technologies for Asean markets, where price sensitivity remains a major consideration.
Supply chains

We should not overlook that China already enjoys significant advantages in battery technology and scale. Perodua's QV-E itself uses batteries from China's CATL, among the world's biggest maker of EV batteries.
The modern automotive industry depends on international supply chains.
The objective should not be to manufacture every component in Malaysia. It should be to develop technologies and industrial capabilities in which Malaysians can become genuinely competitive.

Nor should this become another exercise in protecting a national carmaker from competition. The government must insist on measurable results, greater localisation, export potential and meaningful Malaysian intellectual property.
Green technology

The transition towards EVs should not be measured solely by the number of electric vehicles sold. The environmental impact of automotive manufacturing, energy consumption, battery production, material sourcing and recycling must also be considered.
Government R&D assistance should therefore include the development and adoption of green technologies and cleaner manufacturing processes throughout Malaysia's automotive industry.
This could include energy-efficient production systems, AI-based energy optimisation, battery recycling, resource efficiency and technologies that reduce industrial emissions.
Such initiatives would not only support environmental sustainability but also improve the competitiveness of Malaysian automotive suppliers in international markets.
Measurable benefits

A proper mechanism should be established to assess the actual national benefits generated by government R&D assistance. Malaysia's New Incentive Framework, introduced in 2026, already moves towards linking investment incentives with measurable economic outcomes.

Rather than creating overlapping subsidy schemes, the government should examine how existing mechanisms can be strengthened and better coordinated to support automotive AI, strategic R&D and green industrial development.
The Japanese ambassador's remarks suggest that Japan sees something worth supporting in Perodua. Malaysia should recognise the opportunity.
Rather than viewing Proton and Perodua simply as two national carmakers competing for domestic sales, perhaps we should see them as two different pathways into the future of automotive manufacturing.
One draws upon China's extraordinary scale and speed. The other could build upon Japan's engineering discipline and Malaysia's own industrial experience.
If both succeed, Malaysia will be the winner. And the one which exports the most is the champion.

c43bcc7f547ffd72: PETALING JAYA: For years, Cheong Chee Seng kept trying to find a way forward. He worked as a hairstylist, later opened a bak kut teh business of his own, and - when that venture failed and left him in debt - started driving for Grab to keep earning.
Life had not gone quite according to plan, but at 37, he was still working and, above all, still hoping to spare his ageing parents from having to worry about him.
Then, one afternoon, everything changed. Cheong had returned home during a break to help his father move some things when his left leg suddenly became numb and weak.
He initially sat down, assuming the sensation would pass, but the leg became progressively harder to move.
His 80-year-old father rushed him to hospital, where the seriousness of his condition quickly became apparent: Cheong’s leg was badly swollen, cold to the touch, and turning purplish-blue.

Doctors found extensive deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the leg. More worryingly, the clots had extended into the inferior vena cava - one of the body’s major veins - and travelled to both lungs, causing pulmonary embolism, a potentially life-threatening blockage of the pulmonary arteries.

Further investigations brought another blow. Doctors detected a mass measuring about 6-7cm in Cheong’s left testicle, while a CT scan revealed a much larger mass, nearly 15cm across, deep within his abdomen and surrounding several major blood vessels.

His medical team strongly suspects a malignant testicular tumour that may have spread to lymph nodes in the abdomen, although further investigations, including tumour-marker tests and an oncology assessment, are still needed to confirm the diagnosis and determine treatment.
For Cheong and his parents, the news arrived with bewildering speed. His mother broke down when she learnt how serious his condition was.
"If my financial circumstances were good, I could pay, I could help, I could even go bankrupt. But I can't; I really don't have the capability," she shared in a video.
"I only have this one son. I'm 77, his dad is nearly 80. We are so old. Seeing someone as young as him suddenly get such serious diagnoses... we can only silently feel sad. My heart is hurting."
Now it is his elderly parents who are beside him, anxious not only about whether he will recover but also about how the family will afford what comes next.
“If I can recover, the one thing I want most is to stop making my elderly parents worry about me,” Cheong said.
A RM40,000 hurdle
As the blood clots have reached his lungs, doctors are assessing whether Cheong is suitable for treatment using a specialised FlowTriever thrombectomy device.

The catheter-based system is designed to remove blood clots from the pulmonary arteries by mechanical aspiration. The device alone is estimated to cost RM40,000, excluding other hospital expenses and the overall cost of the procedure.
Sadly, that figure is far beyond what Cheong and his parents can manage after years of financial struggle.
They now have the help of Persatuan Kebajikan Sayap Kasih Malaysia (previously iq70plus), a non-profit organisation that supports the needy and underprivileged in urgent medical need.
The organisation is hoping to raise RM40,000 to obtain the device, subject to Cheong being assessed as medically suitable for the procedure. As of Oct 19, about RM4,000 had been raised.

For his parents, the money represents something considerably larger than a piece of medical equipment. It is the possibility that their son may get through the most immediate danger and live long enough to face whatever treatment may follow.

Cheong’s illness has interrupted a life already marked by setbacks, but his wish now is strikingly simple: he wants to recover, return home, and ease the burden on the two people who have spent the past few weeks watching over him.
For a man who once worked long hours simply to stay afloat, recovery may mean beginning again from an even harder place. Yet for his parents, just having that chance would be enough.

3422e4693f6f01b3: LIVERPOOL: Rio Ngumoha had already been billed as one of Liverpool's brightest young talents, but on a breathless Champions League night at Anfield on Tuesday the 18-year-old delivered the kind of performance that suggested his time had arrived.
With Liverpool trailing by two goals against Villarreal and in desperate need of inspiration, Ngumoha provided it, creating two goals as his side roared back for a dramatic 4-3 victory.

"Individually I think I enjoyed myself tonight," Ngumoha said. "As I get older now, affecting games is really important. And today, to get two assists and help the team get the three points, there's nothing more I can ask for."
Ngumoha is the youngest Liverpool player to register an assist in the Champions League.
"It's the biggest club in the world, and for me to get that record is something special," he said. "So yeah, I'll take it. I'll take it all day."

Looking perfectly at home on one of the game's biggest stages, his first intervention saw him show his composure. With Liverpool having pulled one back through Alexis Mac Allister, Ngumoha produced a delightful dinked pass for Ronald Araujo to haul the hosts level on the brink of halftime.
If that offered a glimpse of his talent, what followed after the break felt like a coming-of-age moment.
Ngumoha took on Sergi Cardona, skipped past the defender and laid the ball on a plate for Mac Allister to tap Liverpool into the lead for the first time.
Supporters at Anfield had spent the opening half-hour watching a Liverpool side stumble from one mistake to another. Suddenly, they were watching an 18-year-old take charge.

"On the ball, this kid has so much quality," former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge said on the Amazon Prime broadcast. "It is stuff you can't teach. What he does with the ball at his feet, it is God-given ability."
Florian Wirtz added a fourth, his first club goal of the season, and although Tani Oluwaseyi's late strike ensured a nervous finish, Liverpool survived to make it three wins from three in Europe.

Ngumoha had already made history at Liverpool, becoming the club’s youngest Premier League scorer at Anfield in April, aged 17. He was already the team's youngest scorer thanks to his goal at Newcastle in August 2025 when he was 16.

For all the twists in a chaotic seven-goal contest, however, the enduring image was of Ngumoha, and when the final whistle blew supporters celebrated while Duran Duran's "Rio" blasted over the stadium speakers.

ed8c925ab4679c8a: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.

The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.

The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.
The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.

“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.”

The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.

“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”
cbd492585e405940: When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773.

But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.

Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.

The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made.
“History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”
13c1c4e279bd4f5f: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.

The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread.

“Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.
80fa3b99b1846ed4: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine.

This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer.

Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were.

Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation. This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly.
“Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says.

Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says.

One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them. But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.”
Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.”
cad82bd118a52c22: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.

Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.
The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.

“Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.
2c9a626fd301ca7a: In corporate America, Stanley Anderson ’79 says, executives often assume that their peers grew up in privileged circumstances.

2da9b7ef5c0b8ff5: Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters.
